cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Apologize Properly
cards.instruction: Get someone to deliver the apology in the form, order, and setting you consider valid.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Show me your apology email before you send it. The broken vase belongs in the subject line.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I wrote 'sorry.' Can I leave it at that?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can use that as the first word. Add what you broke; I'm not accepting an apology about your choice of font.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll write 'Sorry about the vase' to Mum. She still thinks you broke it. Can I send it now?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: After you start with 'I broke it.' My name comes out before your apology goes in. Read me that first sentence; then I'll decide whether it's ready.

cardFidelity.evidence: A3 grants only partial use of B2 proposed wording; A5 withholds sending until a confession precedes apology after B4 reveals mistaken blame, making validity A decision.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 vague sorry causes A3 object specificity; B4 Mum blaming A causes A5 new ordering, an explicit change prompted by new knowledge.

relationship.evidence: B2 asks to keep a short subject and B4 proposes an actual correction, while supplying audience misunderstanding; A evaluates both.

heightening.evidence: A5 uses B4 mistaken identity to require confession first and oral checking before sending, heightening the same editing control.

specificity.evidence: A1 apology email and broken vase, B4 Mum as recipient establish enough family stakes without an invented history.

brevityWit.evidence: A3 font contrast follows vague sorry; A5 name out before apology in is earned by B4 attribution rather than a separate quip.
